title: Alka-Seltzer Plus and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Every Version Checked
excerpt: Can you drink on Alka-Seltzer Plus? Which versions contain aspirin, acetaminophen, or drowsy antihistamines, why each clashes with alcohol, how long to wait, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Alka-Seltzer Plus? Which versions have aspirin, acetaminophen, or drowsy antihistamines, how long to wait, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's best not to drink while you're taking Alka-Seltzer Plus. Every version contains at least one ingredient whose own label warns about alcohol. The fizzy tablets usually contain **aspirin**, which raises the risk of stomach bleeding when combined with alcohol. Many of the liquid gels contain **acetaminophen** (the drug in Tylenol), which can damage the liver when combined with heavy drinking. The night-time versions add a **sedating antihistamine**, and alcohol makes that drowsiness much stronger. A single drink several hours after one daytime dose is unlikely to hurt a healthy adult, but the safest plan is simple: skip alcohol until you're done with the medicine and feeling better.

**The quick rules:** Check the Drug Facts box to see whether your box uses aspirin or acetaminophen, because that decides which organ is at risk. Never drink on the same night you take a "Night" version. Don't combine Alka-Seltzer Plus with Tylenol, NyQuil, DayQuil, or another multi-symptom cold product. If you have 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using any Alka-Seltzer Plus product.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using Alka-Seltzer Plus if** you drink 3 or more alcoholic drinks most days, have liver disease, have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, take a blood thinner or daily aspirin, take an antidepressant (especially an MAOI), have high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, glaucoma, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate, are on a low-sodium diet, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US)** if someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, or passing black, tarry stools. **Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US)** if you think you took more than the label allows, even if you feel fine.

## Why Alka-Seltzer Plus and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Interaction in Plain Words

Alka-Seltzer Plus isn't one drug. It's a family of multi-symptom cold and flu medicines from Bayer, and each one combines two to four active ingredients. That's why there's no single answer to "is it safe with alcohol." The answer depends on which ingredients are in your box. The good news is that the ingredients fall into a small number of groups, and each group has a clear, label-backed alcohol problem.

### 1. The pain reliever: aspirin or acetaminophen

Every Alka-Seltzer Plus cold product includes a pain reliever and fever reducer. It's one of two:

- **Aspirin.** Aspirin is an NSAID (the same family as ibuprofen and naproxen). It works partly by blocking substances called prostaglandins, and some of those prostaglandins protect the stomach lining. Aspirin also makes platelets, the blood cells that start clots, less sticky for days. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining on its own. Put the two together and you get a lining that's more irritated and a body that's slower to stop any bleeding. That's why US aspirin labels carry a stomach-bleeding warning for people who have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product.
- **Acetaminophen.** Your liver breaks down acetaminophen, and a small slice of each dose turns into a toxic by-product. The liver neutralizes it with an antioxidant called glutathione. Regular heavy drinking ramps up the enzyme that makes the toxic by-product and drains glutathione, so the safety margin shrinks. US acetaminophen labels warn that severe liver damage may occur if you have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product. We cover this in depth in our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

### 2. The antihistamine (in some versions)

Some versions contain a first-generation antihistamine, usually **chlorpheniramine** or **doxylamine**. These dry up a runny nose and sneezing, but they also cross into the brain and cause drowsiness. Doxylamine is sedating enough that it's sold on its own as a sleep aid. Alcohol is also a sedative, and the two add up. The antihistamine labels say plainly: alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness, so avoid alcoholic drinks. The combined effect can mean slower reactions, poor coordination, dizziness, and in larger amounts, dangerously deep sleep. For more on this group, see our guide to [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol).

### 3. The cough suppressant (in some versions)

Many "Cold & Flu" and "Night" versions include **dextromethorphan**, often shortened to DXM. At label doses it quiets the cough reflex. It also causes dizziness and drowsiness in some people, and alcohol can make those effects stronger. Taken in large amounts, DXM causes serious impairment on its own, and adding alcohol raises that risk.

### 4. The decongestant: phenylephrine

Most Alka-Seltzer Plus cold products contain **phenylephrine**, a decongestant meant to shrink swollen nasal passages. It doesn't have a major direct interaction with alcohol, but two things are worth knowing. First, it can raise blood pressure and heart rate in some people, and a night of drinking can do the same. Second, in 2023 an FDA advisory panel concluded that oral phenylephrine, at the doses used in over-the-counter products, is not effective as a decongestant, and the FDA has since proposed removing it from the list of approved oral decongestant ingredients. So it may not be doing much for your stuffy nose anyway.

### 5. The fizz: sodium bicarbonate and citric acid

The effervescent tablets fizz because they contain sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and citric acid. This makes them dissolve fast and taste less like a pill, but it also adds a meaningful amount of sodium to each dose. That matters if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, or if you're on a low-sodium diet. It isn't an alcohol interaction as such, but drinking can raise blood pressure too, so it's another reason to be careful.

## Alka-Seltzer Plus Versions and Alcohol: A Quick Comparison

Bayer sells many Alka-Seltzer Plus products, and the line-up and formulas change over time. The table below groups them by the kind of ingredients they *typically* contain. **Always read the Drug Facts box on your actual package**, because that's the only reliable source for what you're taking.

| Version type | Usual pain reliever | Drowsy antihistamine? | Other common ingredients | Main alcohol concern |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cold, original fizzy tablets | Aspirin | Yes (chlorpheniramine) | Phenylephrine | Stomach bleeding, extra drowsiness |
| Night cold, fizzy tablets | Aspirin | Yes (doxylamine) | Dextromethorphan, phenylephrine | Strong sedation, stomach bleeding |
| Day or "non-drowsy" cold and flu | Often acetaminophen (check) | No | Dextromethorphan, phenylephrine, sometimes guaifenesin | Liver strain, dizziness |
| Severe Cold & Flu liquid gels (day) | Acetaminophen | No | Dextromethorphan, guaifenesin, phenylephrine | Liver strain, hidden acetaminophen |
| Severe Cold & Flu liquid gels (night) | Acetaminophen | Yes (doxylamine) | Dextromethorphan, phenylephrine | Strong sedation plus liver strain |
| Original Alka-Seltzer (not "Plus") | Aspirin | No | Sodium bicarbonate, citric acid | Stomach bleeding, sodium load |
| Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief | Aspirin | No | Caffeine | Stomach bleeding |

Two patterns stand out. If the box says **"Night"**, it almost always contains a sedating antihistamine, and you shouldn't drink that night at all. If the box is a **liquid gel**, it's more likely to contain acetaminophen, so you need to count it toward your daily acetaminophen total.

## Alka-Seltzer Plus Cold and Alcohol

The original Alka-Seltzer Plus Cold formula, the fizzy tablet most people picture, combines aspirin, chlorpheniramine, and phenylephrine. With alcohol, you're stacking two concerns. The aspirin and alcohol together irritate the stomach and raise the chance of bleeding. The chlorpheniramine and alcohol together make you drowsier than either would alone.

Chlorpheniramine is less sedating than doxylamine, so the "day" feel of this version can trick people into thinking it's fine to have a drink with dinner. It's still labeled with the alcohol warning, and it can still slow your reactions. Don't drive or operate anything dangerous after combining them.

If you've already taken a dose and then had a single drink, don't panic. For a healthy adult who doesn't drink heavily, that's unlikely to cause serious harm. Stop at one, drink water, eat something, don't take another dose until the alcohol has cleared, and watch for the warning signs listed further down.

## Alka-Seltzer Plus Night and Alcohol

The night versions are the riskiest to mix with alcohol. They're built to knock you out so you can sleep through a cold, which usually means **doxylamine** plus **dextromethorphan**, on top of either aspirin or acetaminophen. Alcohol adds a third sedating ingredient to the mix.

What that can look like in practice:

- Feeling much more drunk or groggy than the amount you drank would suggest
- Dizziness, unsteadiness, and falls, especially getting up at night
- Deeper, harder-to-wake sleep, which is a real concern if you vomit while asleep
- Next-morning grogginess that lasts well past the usual hangover

Older adults, people who are small or light, and people who also take other sedating medicines such as sleep aids, anxiety medicines, or opioid painkillers are at higher risk. If you need a night-time cold medicine, take it on a night you're not drinking. If you've been drinking, pick a non-drowsy option or skip it and rely on rest and fluids. The same logic applies to [NyQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol).

## Alka-Seltzer Plus Severe Cold & Flu and Alcohol

The "Severe" and "Maximum Strength" liquid gels are where hidden acetaminophen becomes the main issue. A typical dose of these products contains acetaminophen along with dextromethorphan, phenylephrine, and either guaifenesin (to loosen mucus) for the day version or doxylamine for the night version.

The danger here isn't usually one dose and one drink. It's the combination of:

- **Repeated doses** across a few days of being sick
- **Doubling up** with Tylenol, NyQuil, DayQuil, Theraflu, or a store-brand cold medicine, many of which also contain acetaminophen
- **Not eating much** because you feel unwell, which lowers the liver's glutathione supply
- **Regular heavy drinking**, which shrinks the liver's safety margin further

Accidental acetaminophen overdoses often happen exactly this way, with several products taken over several days. On labels, look for **acetaminophen**, **APAP**, or **paracetamol**. Add up every dose from every product. If you're unsure of your total, call a pharmacist or Poison Control. We break down the similar problem with [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol) and [Theraflu and alcohol](/never-hungover/theraflu-and-alcohol).

## How Long After Taking Alka-Seltzer Plus Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours for everyone is guessing. A few sensible guidelines:

- **Wait at least until the dose wears off.** Most Alka-Seltzer Plus products are dosed every 4 to 6 hours. Waiting out that window is a reasonable minimum for daytime versions.
- **Wait longer after night versions.** Doxylamine can leave you drowsy well into the next morning. Don't drink the same night, and be cautious the next day if you still feel foggy.
- **The safest choice is to wait until you've stopped the medicine.** Most colds clear up within about a week to 10 days. If you're sick enough to need a multi-symptom cold medicine, your body will recover faster without alcohol anyway.
- **Going the other direction**, if you've been drinking and want to take Alka-Seltzer Plus, wait until the alcohol has cleared. Your body handles roughly one standard drink an hour, though that varies a lot between people. After a heavy night, that can take well into the next day.

If you drink heavily on a regular basis, the waiting time matters less than the pattern. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using either the aspirin or acetaminophen versions.

## Can You Take Alka-Seltzer Plus for a Hangover?

People sometimes reach for whatever Alka-Seltzer is in the cupboard the morning after. Alka-Seltzer Plus isn't a good choice for a hangover, for three reasons:

1. **You'd be taking drugs you don't need.** A hangover isn't a cold. Decongestants, antihistamines, and cough suppressants do nothing for a hangover and add side effects like drowsiness, dry mouth, and a racing heart.
2. **Antihistamines can make you feel worse.** Grogginess and dry mouth are already part of a hangover, and a sedating antihistamine adds to both.
3. **It only treats the headache.** The pain reliever might help your headache, but there's no good evidence that any Alka-Seltzer product fixes the other parts of a hangover, such as fatigue, poor sleep, or the general unwell feeling.

If all you have is a headache, a single plain pain reliever, taken with food and water once the alcohol has cleared, is the simpler choice. Our guides to [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) and the original [Alka-Seltzer for hangovers](/never-hungover/alka-seltzer-for-hangover) explain the trade-offs between the aspirin products. Never take any pain reliever before bed "just in case." You're adding a drug while your body is still processing alcohol, often on an empty stomach.

## What If You're Sick and Have Plans to Drink?

Colds tend to arrive right before weddings, holidays, and birthdays. If you're set on having a drink while you're under the weather, these steps lower the risk:

- **Choose your medicine around the drinking, not the other way round.** Skip any "Night" product that evening. If you need something, a single-ingredient option for your worst symptom is easier to manage than a four-in-one formula.
- **Keep it to one or two drinks** and space them out with water. Your body is already working to fight the infection.
- **Eat a real meal.** Food protects your stomach and helps your liver.
- **Don't take a dose right before you go out or right before bed after drinking.** Leave a gap of several hours on each side.
- **Don't drive** if you've combined any cold medicine with alcohol, even if you feel okay.

It's also worth knowing that alcohol won't help you get over a cold. It dehydrates you and disrupts the deep sleep your immune system relies on. Our piece on [whether alcohol helps a cold](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-help-a-cold) covers this, and if you're looking for options that don't contain alcohol themselves, see our [alcohol-free cold medicine](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine) guide.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining Alka-Seltzer Plus and alcohol if you:

- Drink **3 or more drinks most days**, or binge regularly
- Have **liver disease**, hepatitis, fatty liver, or elevated liver enzymes (acetaminophen versions)
- Have had a **stomach ulcer, stomach bleeding, or ongoing heartburn** (aspirin versions)
- Take a **blood thinner**, daily aspirin, other NSAIDs, steroids, or certain antidepressants (SSRIs or SNRIs), all of which raise bleeding risk with aspirin
- Take **other sedating medicines**, such as sleep aids, anxiety medicines, muscle relaxants, or opioid painkillers
- Take an **MAOI antidepressant**, or stopped one in the last two weeks. Labels for products containing dextromethorphan or phenylephrine say not to use them with MAOIs.
- Have **high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, or diabetes** (phenylephrine and the sodium in fizzy tablets can be a concern)
- Are **older**, since sedating antihistamines raise the risk of confusion and falls in older adults
- Are under 18 or giving the medicine to a teenager. Aspirin products carry a warning about Reye's syndrome in children and teens recovering from flu or chickenpox.

If any of these apply, a five-minute chat with a pharmacist is worth it. They can look at your full medication list and suggest a cold remedy that fits. For a broader look at how common medicines interact with supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink after a dose of cold medicine end up feeling drowsy or queasy and nothing more. But a few signs mean you should stop waiting it out.

**Call 911 (US) or go to the emergency room if someone:**

- Is very hard to wake, or can't stay awake
- Is breathing slowly, irregularly, or making gurgling sounds
- Has vomited and is too drowsy to protect their airway
- Vomits blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
- Passes black, tarry, or bloody stools
- Has a seizure, severe confusion, or chest pain

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if:**

- You may have taken more than the labeled dose, or combined several products and aren't sure of the total
- You took acetaminophen-containing products for several days while drinking and now feel unwell

**See a doctor soon if you notice:**

- Ongoing stomach pain or worsening heartburn after taking aspirin versions
- Pain under your right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine, which can signal liver injury after acetaminophen versions
- A cold that lasts longer than about 10 days, a high fever, or symptoms that improve and then get worse

Early acetaminophen poisoning can feel like nothing much: some nausea, sweating, and feeling generally unwell. That's easy to confuse with a hangover or the flu. If an overdose is possible, don't wait for symptoms. Hospital treatment works best when it starts early.

## Safer Ways to Get Through a Cold When You've Been Drinking

If you've already had a few drinks and feel a cold coming on, the basics work better than any combination product:

- **Fluids first.** Water, broth, and warm drinks help with congestion and replace what alcohol took out.
- **Rest.** Go to bed early and skip the nightcap.
- **Salt-water gargles and saline nasal rinses** can ease a sore throat and stuffy nose without any drug interactions.
- **Honey** in warm water or tea can soothe a cough in adults.
- **Target one symptom at a time** the next day, once the alcohol has cleared, rather than taking a product with four ingredients you may not need.

## A Note on Supporting Your Body Around Drinking

Alka-Seltzer Plus treats cold symptoms. It does nothing for alcohol's effects, and in some versions it adds to the work your stomach or liver has to do. If you've found this page because you often drink while also reaching for medicine the next day, the most effective step is still the plain one: **drink less, drink slower, and eat and hydrate properly.** Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. It doesn't make it safe to combine alcohol with cold medicine, and there's no good evidence that it protects against the stomach or liver risks described above. If you want to try it on a night you're not taking medication, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and if you take any regular medication, check with your pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Every Alka-Seltzer Plus product has at least one ingredient with an alcohol warning on its label.
- **Aspirin versions** (many fizzy tablets) raise the risk of stomach bleeding with alcohol. **Acetaminophen versions** (many liquid gels) raise the risk of liver damage with heavy drinking.
- **Night versions** contain a sedating antihistamine. Don't drink the same night you take one.
- Don't stack Alka-Seltzer Plus with Tylenol, NyQuil, DayQuil, or other cold medicines. Check every label for duplicate ingredients.
- If you've had one drink after one daytime dose, stop there, drink water, eat, and wait before the next dose.
- If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or vomiting blood, call 911. If an overdose is possible, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Alka-Seltzer Plus?**

It's best not to. Every Alka-Seltzer Plus product contains at least one ingredient whose label warns about alcohol: aspirin (stomach bleeding), acetaminophen (liver damage), or a drowsy antihistamine (extra sedation). One drink a few hours after a single daytime dose is unlikely to cause harm in a healthy adult, but the safer choice while you're sick is to skip alcohol until you've stopped taking the medicine. If you have 3 or more drinks a day, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using it at all.

**How long after taking Alka-Seltzer Plus can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting time. A practical guide is to wait until the dose has worn off, which for most Alka-Seltzer Plus products means the 4 to 6 hour dosing window on the label, and longer for night-time versions that cause drowsiness. Waiting until you've finished the medicine entirely, and you're feeling better, is the safest option. Ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have liver, stomach, or bleeding problems.

**Is Alka-Seltzer Plus Night safe with alcohol?**

No, night versions are the worst ones to combine with alcohol. They contain doxylamine, a sedating antihistamine, and the label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks because alcohol increases the drowsiness. Many also contain dextromethorphan plus either aspirin or acetaminophen. Together with alcohol, that can mean heavy sedation, poor coordination, and slowed reactions. Don't drink the same night you take a night-time cold medicine.

**Does Alka-Seltzer Plus have aspirin or acetaminophen?**

It depends on the version. Many of the fizzy effervescent tablets, including the original Alka-Seltzer Plus Cold formula, use aspirin. Many of the liquid gels, including the Severe Cold and Flu products, use acetaminophen. Check the Drug Facts box on your package, because formulas vary and change over time. This matters because aspirin and alcohol raise the risk of stomach bleeding, while acetaminophen and alcohol raise the risk of liver damage.

**Can I take Alka-Seltzer Plus for a hangover?**

It isn't designed for one. Alka-Seltzer Plus is a cold medicine, so you'd be taking decongestants, antihistamines, or cough suppressants you don't need. If all you have is a headache, a single plain pain reliever taken with food and water after the alcohol has cleared is a simpler choice. There's also a separate product, Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief, which contains aspirin and caffeine and carries its own stomach-bleeding warning.

**Can I take Alka-Seltzer Plus with Tylenol or NyQuil?**

Be very careful. Many Alka-Seltzer Plus liquid gels already contain acetaminophen, the active ingredient in Tylenol and in NyQuil. Taking them together can push you over the daily limit without realizing it, and that risk is higher if you've been drinking. Aspirin-based versions shouldn't be stacked with ibuprofen or naproxen either. Use one multi-symptom product at a time and check every label for duplicate ingredients.

**Does alcohol make a cold worse?**

Alcohol doesn't cure a cold and can make recovery harder. It dehydrates you, disrupts the deep sleep your body needs to recover, and can worsen congestion for some people. Combined with cold medicine, it adds drowsiness and stomach or liver risk. Water, rest, and warm fluids are better choices until you feel better.
